Can Vera Rubin run accurate 3-bit LLM inference?

We study one question: can Rubin's native LUT-B instruction run 3-bit model weights and 3-bit KV cache without destroying model quality?

14 min read

Answer: Yes! Reaching production-grade quality requires precise algorithm and quantizer design. A naive 3-bit codebook can increase perplexity by thousands of times. The algorithm, not the bit width alone, decides whether INT3 works.

Rubin LUT-B

What the kernel does

A native decompress::lut::b MMA multiplies an E4M3 A tile by a compressed B tile [8]. Each B element is stored as a 3-bit index selecting one of eight E4M3 reconstruction values in Tensor Memory. Lookup and multiplication happen inside the tensor-core instruction, so the kernel never materializes a dense BF16 or FP16 B matrix.

How the kernel computes the product

The mathematical operation is still \(Y=A\cdot B\). For one K block, read the implementation from left to right:

\[ \mathrm{index} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{LUT}} B_q, \qquad D=\operatorname{MMA}(A_q,B_q), \qquad \Delta Y=D\times s_A\times s_B\times g, \qquad Y\leftarrow Y+\Delta Y . \]

Here \(A_q\approx A_{\mathrm{real}}/s_A\) and \(B_q\approx B_{\mathrm{real}}/(g\,s_B)\) are the small E4M3 operands. The 3-bit index chooses the normalized B value \(B_q\); the scale does not choose a LUT entry—it restores that entry's magnitude. For two K32 halves, the same rule becomes:

\[ \Delta Y[m,n] = g\sum_{h=0}^{1} D_h[m,n]\, s_A[m,h]\, s_B[n,h]. \]

The diagram shows exactly which values share a LUT or a scale. Native LUT-B consumes one K64 compressed block, so the simplest path uses one scale per K64×N1 column group and one K64 MMA. Finer K32 scales can improve accuracy, but there is no ready-made K32 LUT-B MMA. We therefore either run two masked K64 MMAs, one for each half, or combine the A and B scales inside one block-scaled K64 MMA when the descriptor supports it.

Swipe horizontally to compare all three scale layouts →

Item Where it lives How it is used Optional?
3-bit index + 8-value LUT Stored in the offline B payload Reconstructs the E4M3 B value inside LUT-B No
\(s_A\) Generated online for each A row and K block Multiplies the MMA partial to undo A quantization Used in W3A8/K3V3; otherwise \(s_A=1\)
\(s_B\) Stored with each B tile, output column, and K block/half Multiplies the MMA partial to restore weight/cache range Recipe-dependent; otherwise \(s_B=1\)
\(g\) One FP32 value per tensor Multiplied once with the accumulated output Optional; otherwise \(g=1\)
  1. Tile A and B. One 128-thread CTA owns one M128×N8 output tile and traverses K in 64-element segments. A rows are quantized online to E4M3 with their UE8M0 block scales, while the B payload is already packed offline.
  2. Stage one K64 payload. The CTA copies the 256-byte native B image into shared memory, loads the matching eight-value LUT, and stages each thread's A fragment plus replicated LUT data in Tensor Memory. Synchronization makes the descriptors visible before issue.
  3. Issue and wait. One thread issues tcgen05.mma…decompress::lut::b; hardware performs the 3-bit lookup and E4M3 multiply while accumulating FP32 D. The CTA commits the MMA to an mbarrier and waits before reading D from Tensor Memory.
  4. Restore and accumulate. The kernel multiplies D by \(s_A\times s_B\), adds it to Y, and applies optional \(g\). The current correctness kernel performs these multiplies in the FP32 epilogue; a compatible block-scale MMA can apply the separable \(s_A\times s_B\) product inside the instruction.

Two challenges

  1. How to preserve accuracy at three bits. Eight reconstruction values must cover weight or KV distributions with severe outliers. The codebook, K64/K32 scale granularity, E4M3 A rounding, optional global factor, and calibration objective all move PPL/KL. The central algorithmic problem is choosing these pieces together without spending the byte savings on metadata or extra passes.
  2. How to utilize the hardware efficiently. LUT-B decompresses only B, which constrains operand orientation. Its M tile has 128 rows, while batch-1 GQA or one routed expert may expose only a few useful rows. A production kernel must combine a compatible B-side schedule with request batching or expert gathering, overlap payload movement with MMA, and move separable scale products into the block-scaled instruction instead of reading every partial back in software.

Challenge 1 — Our accuracy algorithm

Weight path

We pack static \(W^\top\) once and quantize each activation row to E4M3 online. The compared algorithms change the offline payload:

  1. Condition outliers with optional H64 or AWQ.
  2. Fit eight E4M3 values using Lloyd–Max [1,2], RMS² weighting, or Fisher-weighted SqueezeLLM [5].
  3. Optionally apply Hessian-guided GPTQ compensation [3] or alternate GPTQ with codebook refitting.
  4. Select K64, two-K32, and optional tensor-global scales.
  5. Pack indices/LUT/scales and execute one LUT-B GEMM per linear layer or routed expert.

Weight papers and method families tested

  • Codebook baselines: uniform INT3, fixed NF3, and learned Lloyd–Max [1,2].
  • Calibration objectives: activation RMS² weighting and SqueezeLLM-style diagonal-Fisher weighting [5].
  • Second-order correction: GPTQ [3] and our inter-GPTQ loop, which alternates GPTQ compensation with LUT refitting.
  • Outlier conditioning: QuaRot-style signed H64 [6] and AWQ channel scaling [4], folded only where the RMSNorm fan-out permits it.
  • Scale contracts: LUT-only, native K64 UE8M0, two-K32, and optional tensor-global scaling.

KV path

We keep sensitive sink/recent tokens in BF16 and seal older Kᵀ and V once into LUT-B payloads:

  1. Fit per-layer Lloyd–Max codebooks [1,2]; optionally condition K/V with OSCAR [7].
  2. Quantize Q to E4M3 and execute Q×Kᵀ through LUT-B.
  3. Keep max, exponentiation, sum, and normalization in FP32.
  4. Quantize P to E4M3 and execute P×V through LUT-B.
  5. Merge the compressed-body result with the BF16 window.

KV-cache papers and method families

  • Codebook baselines: ordinary uniform K3V3, per-layer Lloyd–Max K3V3 [1,2], and the TurboQuant learned-centroid baseline [9].
  • OSCAR [7]: OSCAR+uniform and OSCAR+Lloyd–Max K3V3, plus OSCAR INT2 as a reference.
  • Precision and window ablations: BF16 versus E4M3/UE8M0 Q/P, with sink/recent windows retained or removed.
  • Architectures: separate K/V in GQA/MHA and direct 512-d latent quantization in Kimi K3 Gated-MLA.

Experiment 1 — 3-bit weights

We compare 18 quantized configurations plus BF16 and A8 baselines across Qwen3-4B, Gemma4-12B, and MiniMax-M3 at 8K, 64K, and 128K. The question is whether algorithm choice can make native W3A8 usable.

Real Rubin hardware — full-model native run. We ran Qwen3-4B, Gemma4-12B, and MiniMax-M3 on a physical SM107 Vera Rubin GPU. The selected weights were stored as packed 3-bit indices, eight-value E4M3 LUTs, and UE8M0 scales; the corresponding BF16 weight storage was removed. A CUDA extension replaced each Qwen/Gemma text linear and each selected MiniMax routed-expert W13/W2 multiplication with tcgen05.mma…decompress::lut::b. The reported native PPL/KL therefore comes from complete model forwards on real Rubin silicon, not from fake quantization or a software-unpack fallback; the MiniMax run records zero simulated fallback GEMMs.

What the compared algorithms do

  • Lloyd–Max / uniform / NF3. Uniform spaces eight levels evenly; NF3 uses a fixed normal-inspired codebook; Lloyd–Max [1,2] learns eight centroids from each tile. This isolates whether fitting the codebook matters.
  • RMS² / SqueezeLLM. RMS² weights reconstruction error by activation second moments. SqueezeLLM [5] instead uses diagonal Fisher information. Both change the codebook fit; neither is GPTQ compensation.
  • GPTQ / inter-GPTQ. GPTQ [3] uses a block Hessian to push each rounding error into columns not yet quantized. Inter-GPTQ alternates this compensation sweep with refitting the eight-value codebook.
  • H64 / AWQ / scale variants. H64 follows the rotated-quantization idea in QuaRot [6], spreading outliers with a signed Hadamard transform and applying the matching transform to A. AWQ [4] rescales activation channels and folds the inverse scale into weights; K64/two-K32/global variants change scale granularity.

Every reported quantized GEMM runs through the native Rubin LUT-B MMA.

Result — Qwen and Gemma. The plain Lloyd–Max baseline increases PPL by 43.7% on Qwen and 1,430% on Gemma. Our best method family is Hadamard+GPTQ with a refitted LUT codebook; its best native variants reduce the PPL penalty to 21.2% on Qwen and 20.3% on Gemma. Relative to plain Lloyd–Max, those selected variants also reduce KL₅₀ by 45.6% on Qwen and 88.0% on Gemma. The main dense-model result is therefore that the baseline 3-bit codebook is not robust, while Hadamard conditioning plus Hessian-guided compensation makes the same LUT-B format usable.

Result — MiniMax-M3. The plain Lloyd–Max baseline increases PPL by 70.1%. The best method is √Fisher+four-restart Lloyd–Max, which limits the PPL penalty to 11.9% and reduces KL₅₀ by 62.6% relative to plain Lloyd–Max. For routed experts, importance-weighted codebook fitting is more effective than adding a Hadamard runtime transform.

Experiment 2 — 3-bit KV cache

Figure 2 compares five Qwen KV configurations (BF16 plus four compressed recipes) and three Kimi latent-cache configurations. It asks whether a fitted codebook and controlled scales can make native K3V3 accurate while reducing cache traffic.

Real Rubin hardware — native Qwen K3V3 attention. On the same physical SM107 GPU, completed Qwen native rows stored the compressed cache body as real 3-bit Kᵀ/V payloads. Each attention layer executed E4M3 Q × LUT-B Kᵀ, FP32 softmax, and E4M3 P × LUT-B V without reconstructing the compressed body as dense BF16 in HBM. PPL/KL was measured through the complete Qwen forward pass, including its BF16 sink/recent window. The Kimi K3 points are numerical latent-cache quality runs rather than native Rubin cache measurements; Figure 2's data-source control keeps those evidence classes separate.

What the KV algorithms do

  • Window and sealing. Sink and recent tokens remain BF16. Older K/V are sealed once in 64-token chunks as 3-bit indices, layer-specific LUT values, and scales; decode never writes them again.
  • Lloyd–Max codebooks. Each layer learns eight non-uniform values from calibration data [1,2], placing resolution where K/V values occur. Uniform levels waste codes on sparse tails and collapse PPL.
  • OSCAR. A calibrated rotation and clipping rule [7] spreads outliers before fitting the codebook. It can improve some models, but adds transforms unless they are absorbed into adjacent projections.
  • Native attention path. E4M3 Q multiplies compressed Kᵀ; max, exp, sum, and normalization stay FP32; E4M3 P then multiplies compressed V. Both cache reads use B-side LUT decompression.

Result — Qwen3-4B: OSCAR wins simulated KL, not every metric. The uniform K3V3 baseline increases PPL by 13,057% relative to BF16. In the controlled simulation, OSCAR+Lloyd–Max has the lowest KL₅₀, reducing it by 1.4% relative to Lloyd–Max alone, while the no-OSCAR method has 0.5% lower PPL. The best completed native result also remains no-OSCAR Lloyd–Max, with an 8.7% PPL penalty relative to BF16; the current native OSCAR run has not reproduced the simulated KL advantage. OSCAR additionally requires a cache rotation and a matching transform unless they are absorbed into adjacent projections.

Result — Kimi K3: OSCAR is the overall winner. Relative to plain Lloyd–Max K3V3, OSCAR+Lloyd–Max reduces PPL by 2.3%, reduces KL₅₀ by 15.1%, and improves GPQA by 6.57 points. The gain is not free: OSCAR adds a latent-cache rotation and a matching transform unless they can be absorbed into adjacent projections.

Challenge 2 — Kernel efficiency: what speedup could W3A8 and K3V3 enable?

The tables put engineering estimates and deliberately aggressive H100-BF16 byte ceilings side by side. The large values are optimistic bounds, not serving measurements.

In the final column, the first value uses Kimi K3's released MXFP4/MXFP8 format as the practical baseline and assumes W3-eligible GEMMs occupy 80% of batch-1 weight-streaming decode latency. The bold values instead normalize against H100 BF16 and assume an 80% / 90% GEMM share:

\[ S_{\mathrm{engine}}(f) = \frac{1}{(1-f)+f/S_{\mathrm{GEMM}}}. \]

The H64 row uses a 5–7% proxy range consistent with QuaRot's reported at-most-7% online-Hadamard overhead [6], not a Rubin measurement.

AWQ caveat — fold coverage determines speed. AWQ is free only when every inverse channel scale can be absorbed into a compatible affine RMSNorm and all consumers share that fold. The current folded evaluation simply leaves unsupported paths unscaled; applying AWQ to those paths in an engine requires either fusing the rescale into A8 packing or launching another elementwise kernel. The 2–5% and 10–20% ranges above are engineering estimates, not Rubin measurements. In the separate-kernel case, AWQ can cost more than H64 and can erase the remaining gain over Kimi's MXFP4 baseline.

Qwen · Rubin BF16 KV 154.6 GB 142.3 6.57× 3.11× / 4.22×

The Qwen rows model 36-layer GQA4 attention only. The 320-token BF16 sink/recent window makes the effective 1M cache 3.129 bit/value rather than exactly 3.125. The Kimi row is a latent-cache byte normalization rather than a Qwen tok/s projection: only its 512-d latent is compressed, while the 64-d RoPE suffix stays BF16. The end-to-end column is an Amdahl sensitivity that assumes attention occupies 80% or 90% of H100 baseline latency and leaves the rest unchanged.

OSCAR caveat — the table does not subtract rotation cost. The listed ceilings apply to no-OSCAR K3V3 or to an OSCAR rotation that is fully absorbed into adjacent projections. Otherwise, each cache vector must be rotated when sealed and a matching transform must be applied on the QK/PV side. If those transforms add 5–10% to total engine latency, the Qwen 4.47× / 7.89× ceiling falls to 4.06–4.26× / 7.17–7.51×, while Kimi's 4.26× / 7.19× falls to 3.87–4.06× / 6.54–6.85×. The 5–10% range is a sensitivity assumption, not a Rubin measurement.

Conclusion 1 — W3A8. The aggressive upper bound is 32.3× for the eligible weight kernel versus H100 BF16, translating to 4.45× end-to-end at 80% GEMM share or 7.82× at 90%. The more deployment-relevant comparison is smaller because Kimi K3 already uses MXFP4: plain K64 projects to 1.23× and H64 to 1.17–1.19×. AWQ is the fragile case: with the current two-K32 schedule it is about 1.11× only when fully folded, but an unfused runtime rescale lowers the estimate to 0.96–1.03×, eliminating the speedup and potentially making the engine slower.

Conclusion 2 — K3V3. At 1M context, the aggressive Qwen ceiling is 33.6× attention-only versus H100 BF16, or 4.47× / 7.89× end-to-end when attention is 80% / 90% of baseline latency. Kimi K3's latent-only ceiling is 23.0× locally and 4.26× / 7.19× end-to-end under the same assumptions. These are byte ceilings; actual speed still depends on LUT-B rate, small-M scheduling, communication, and OSCAR's rotation cost.
